analysis.one_liner: Lets private employers offer paid time off instead of cash overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 157 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, but never received a committee vote or floor action before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal overtime rules so private employers could offer workers 1.5 hours of paid time off for every overtime hour worked, instead of the overtime cash pay the law now requires. The worker would have to agree in advance, in writing or through a union contract, and could not be pressured into it. Unused time would be capped at 160 hours and cashed out at the end of the year at the higher of the worker's starting or ending pay rate, with payment also due when a worker leaves the job. Workers could ask for cash instead at any time, with 30 days for the employer to pay, and the whole setup would have expired after five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers who would rather have time off than the extra cash, especially parents and caregivers who can plan around employer-approved dates. Employers also gain, because they could hold the overtime money for up to a year and cover staffing gaps with comp time instead of hiring or paying out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers who want time off

how_it_helps.text: Workers could accrue one and a half hours of paid time off for each overtime hour worked, instead of receiving overtime cash pay.

The agreement had to be made before the work was performed, in writing, knowingly and voluntarily, and not as a condition of employment, and employers were barred from intimidating or coercing workers over the choice, with double-rate damages for violations.
Unused comp time had to be cashed out by the end of the year at the higher of the worker's regular rate when earned or the final regular rate, and paid out in full on termination of employment.
A worker could withdraw the agreement or request cash for all accrued time at any time, with the employer required to pay within 30 days.
The program would have expired after five years, with the Government Accountability Office reporting to Congress on participation, complaints, and enforcement every three years.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who need the overtime cash now bear the risk of deferral: the employer decides when accrued time can actually be used, and can force a cash-out of hours above 80 or drop the policy with 30 days' notice. Employers bear the bookkeeping and liability for compliance.

drawbacks.text: An employer could refuse a worker's request to use accrued time off if using it would 'unduly disrupt' operations, so the time off is not guaranteed when the worker wants it.

The employer could force payment for unused hours above 80 at any time with 30 days' notice, and could discontinue the comp-time policy entirely with 30 days' notice, leaving workers with the cash they had given up flexibility to avoid.
The agreement changes only how overtime is paid, not whether overtime is worked; the employer, not the employee, decides when overtime hours occur.

Protections depend on individual workers filing complaints and the Labor Department acting on them; oversight consisted of periodic GAO reports on complaints and enforcement, not an automatic employer obligation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker with predictable schedules and a flexible employer, trading overtime cash for guaranteed paid time off is a real benefit. But the same design gives the employer control over when the time can be used, defers the cash for up to a year, and allows the arrangement to be ended on a month's notice, so a worker who needs the money or cannot get time approved can end up worse off than under straight cash overtime. The written-consent, anti-coercion, and year-end cash-out rules limit the risk without removing it, and the five-year sunset plus mandatory GAO reporting showed the sponsors themselves were unsure how it would play out.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its Workforce Protections Subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 22, 2015 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 29, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
All 157 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on.
Even with the committee chairman among its cosponsors, the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hourly workers kept the existing guarantee of cash overtime pay, which opponents of comp time view as the stronger protection; employers who wanted the scheduling and cash-flow flexibility gained nothing, since the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers kept cash overtime; employers gained nothing

for.name: Martha Roby
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered cosponsors.

for.name: 157 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Democrat did.

for.name: John Kline
for.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as chairman never scheduled a committee vote; the bill was referred to a subcommittee in April 2015 and went no further.

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: His administration had recommended a veto of the near-identical House comp-time bill that passed in 2013, signaling the White House would block the approach if it reached his desk.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed private-sector comp time legislation, arguing it would let employers postpone overtime pay and pressure workers out of cash they have earned.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican: all 157 cosponsors were Republicans and none of the chamber's Democrats signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where members would have had to take a position.

industries.note: The bill would have let these employers defer overtime cash for up to a year and fill schedules with accrued comp time, a direct cash-flow benefit. Some of their workers would genuinely have preferred the time off, but the employer controls when that time can be taken.

Comp time competes with cash overtime at the bargaining table and, in unions' view, weakens the guarantee that overtime hours are paid in money. The bill still required a collective bargaining agreement where one exists, but unions opposed the approach for the nonunion workforce it would cover.
